identity.title: The PRISM Alignment Dataset: What Participatory, Representative and Individualised Human Feedback Reveals About the Subjective and Multicultural Alignment of Large Language Models

problem.claim: The paper examines how human feedback for LLM alignment should account for who provides it, where and how feedback is collected, and what objectives it serves.

gap.claim: Existing feedback processes leave open questions about their methods, domains, participants, and objectives.

contributions.claim: Introduces PRISM, mapping sociodemographics and stated preferences of 1,500 participants from 75 countries to contextual preferences and fine-grained feedback in 8,011 live conversations with 21 LLMs.

Provides broader geographic and demographic participation, census-representative samples for the UK and US, and individualised ratings linked to participant profiles for personalisation and attribution of sample artefacts.
Uses PRISM in three case studies focused on subjective, multicultural, value-laden, and controversial alignment perspectives.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors present PRISM as a new dataset combining diverse participant profiles, contextual preferences, and fine-grained feedback across many LLM conversations.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that three case studies demonstrate the need to carefully consider which humans provide alignment data.

narrative_sequence.summary: Human feedback is central to LLM alignment, but key dimensions of feedback processes remain open.
PRISM links diverse participants’ profiles and preferences to detailed feedback from live conversations with 21 LLMs.
The dataset broadens participation, includes UK and US census-representative samples, and supports individualised ratings and attribution of sample artefacts.
Three case studies use PRISM to argue that the selection of humans supplying alignment data requires careful consideration.

source_observation.claim: The abstract connects participant sociodemographics and stated preferences with contextual, individualised feedback, then uses the resource to study subjective and multicultural disagreement.

lessons.interpretation: Alignment claims can be made more informative by preserving who gave feedback and the context in which it was produced.
lessons.application: When building an alignment dataset, record participant profiles and contextual ratings alongside aggregate labels, then analyze whether conclusions vary across people or cultural groups.
lessons.exception: This approach may be unsuitable when collecting or linking demographic profiles creates privacy, consent, or representation risks.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the three case-study designs, quantitative findings, or comparison baselines.
It does not report the extent of interpersonal or cross-cultural disagreement, nor details of the census-representative sampling procedures.
